sections_meta.title: Basic Multi-Agent Reward Schemes and Social Trees
How Verification for BMaRSs is Implemented

summaries.summary: The introduction argues that modern learning algorithms excel as test-takers but lack innovation, suggesting that agent intelligence may be limited by environmental complexity (Leibo et al. 2020).
Arena is built on Unity game engine, which provides desirable features in rendering, physics, customizability, and community support (Juliani et al. 2018).
Arena includes a broadcast board at each node of the social tree to support research in multi-agent communication (Das et al. 2017; Mordatch and Abbeel 2018).
The preliminaries define a Markov game with multiple agents, a global state space, per-agent action spaces, and bounded rewards (Littman 1994).
The paper provides Python implementations of several state-of-the-art baselines for multi-agent algorithm development and validation.
Experiments evaluate the game set across stochasticity, realistic rendering, and simulation speed, with details in the extended version.
Related work surveys multi-agent intelligence research (Hernandez-Leal, Kartal, and Taylor 2018) and reviews competitive and collaborative multi-agent settings.
Verification for BMaRSs is implemented by setting a hyper-parameter N to limit the number of samples enumerated over variable spaces.
Figure 3 illustrates a social tree with BMaRSs applied, and compares self-play (SP) and population-based training (PB) approaches.
Figures 4 and 5 visualize training progress in episode reward and population performance across baselines including D-PPO, SP, and PB.
